title: Every Brilliant Thing review
transcript:
Sitting on stage with Daniel Radcliffe
was an experience I didn't know I needed.
In this solo play,
he tells a coming of age story
about keeping a list of every brilliant thing that's worth living for.
The idea came to him when he was seven,
trying to make sense of why his mother had attempted to take her own life.
From that point on, it became both an anchor and an outlet,
encouraging him to find new ways to appreciate life despite its ups and downs.
The story is pretty straightforward,
told chronologically through monologue.
but there's also a ton of audience participation,
such as people shouting out items from the list,
playing characters in the story,
or even contributing their own belongings as props.
This element adds a lot of humor and spontaneity to the experience,
but it can make the performance feel choppy at times.
There were some moments
when I felt like the audience interactions
were completely gratuitous
and interrupted the emotional through line of the story.
It almost approaches gimmick,
but that's not totally a bad thing.
It just demands a performer who knows how to work a crowd
and is light on their feet.
Daniel Radcliffe fits the Bill perfectly,
giving a performance that significantly elevates what I would not consider
a perfect play.
I was impressed by his ability to tune into the audience and respond accordingly,
while maintaining our attention the entire time
and never dropping the ball on the most important emotional beats.
Even from a Vantage point primarily behind him,
he had us in the palm of his hand.
I would have sat there all night.
I'm happy to answer any questions about the on stage seating,
but there are probably no bad seats for this show.
It's a carefully calibrated experience for everyone in the room.
With that, another Playbill for my collection.
reasoning: The reviewer praises Daniel Radcliffe's performance as significantly elevating the material and describes being captivated, but explicitly notes the play itself is not perfect, calling some audience participation 'gratuitous' and near-gimmicky, with choppy moments that interrupt emotional flow. A clear recommendation with meaningful caveats.
